overview: Nigeria became independent from Britain in 1960 and a federal republic in 1963. Its many language communities built a shared state amid regional conflict. Coups and the Biafran war from 1967 to 1970 devastated families; elected civilian rule returned in 1999 after further military periods. Today Nollywood films, schools and community life show creative energy, while Nigerian health teams helped contain Ebola and wild polio. Oil revenues coexist with severe pollution in parts of the Niger Delta, and many households still need safe water and toilets. The republic and its people continue.

periods.summary: Nigeria became independent in 1960 and a republic in 1963; coups and the Biafran war from 1967 to 1970 brought terrible civilian suffering.

periods.title: Oil, military government and interrupted civilian rule
periods.summary: Oil grew in importance; civilian rule from 1979 to 1983 was followed by further military government and continuing struggles over rights and resources.

periods.title: Civilian democracy and continuing work
periods.summary: A new constitution and elected government began in 1999. Education, film, public health and clean water remain matters of daily life and public debate.

sections.title: An independent country with many voices

items.text: Independence on 1 October 1960 created a self-governing federation. In 1963 a republican constitution replaced the British monarch as head of state. Nigeria’s state changed twice within three years; its communities were much older.

After coups in 1966, the Eastern Region attempted to secede as Biafra in 1967. The war lasted to 1970 and hunger struck civilians. One child later remembered a refugee camp, donated food, medicines and a school uniform for life after the war.

Nigeria had an elected civilian government from 1979 to 1983, then further military rule. Civilian presidential government returned in 1999; the new constitution says political authority belongs to the people.

The country’s languages include Hausa, Igbo, Yoruba, English and hundreds of others. A child can hear one language at home, another at school and a third in a film or market. Language policy aims to support this diversity, although practice varies.

The 1999 constitution begins “We, the people of the Federal Republic of Nigeria.” This short original English sample is from a governing document. Its words promise popular authority; citizens still debate how fully institutions deliver that promise.

sections.title: School, screens and the family table

items.text: Regional free-primary-school efforts began before independence; the federal Universal Basic Education programme followed in 1999. Whether a child can attend regularly still depends on teachers, distance, safety and family resources.

Nollywood grew into a huge film industry, with an estimated 2,500 films a year around 2021. Families may watch a story on a phone or television, then argue about its characters as enthusiastically as any film critic. This is an example of popular culture, not what every household watches.

The Nigerian language policy names several widely used languages and calls for translation and public use beyond English. That matters when a parent tries to understand a school notice, health message or ballot information.

Oil became a major industry after the 1956 Oloibiri discovery. In Ogoniland, a 2011 UN assessment found long-term oil pollution of land and drinking water. A government revenue statistic cannot tell a family whether the nearest well is safe.

In 2014 Nigerian health workers traced contacts, informed communities through local radio and contained an imported Ebola outbreak. WHO declared that outbreak over in October. It took a team, not a miracle.

Vaccination and surveillance helped Nigeria and the African region gain wild-polio-free certification in 2020. This does not mean every form of polio or every childhood health problem vanished; health workers keep checking and vaccinating.

A 2021 national water-and-sanitation survey estimated about 48 million Nigerians still practiced open defecation. A toilet needs safe design, water or maintenance, privacy and a way to wash hands; the answer varies greatly by community.

In parts of the Niger Delta, oil pollution threatens water used for drinking and farming. In some other places, sanitation access is the more immediate challenge. Either way, clean water is part of health, family work and dignity.

ending.text: Nigeria continues as a federal republic. Independence, a new constitution, military interruptions and the return to civilian rule changed its institutions; none ended its older communities or languages. Families continue to build livelihoods, schools, art and healthier neighborhoods while arguing over the country’s future.
